questions.prompt: What is the difference between static (`libx.a`) and dynamic (`libx.so`) libraries?
options: Static code is copied into the executable at link time; dynamic code is loaded when the program runs
Static libraries are slower because they use the network
Dynamic libraries are copied into the executable; static ones are not
There is no difference, only the file name
questions.explain: A statically linked executable carries its own copy of the code it needs. A dynamically linked one needs the `.so` at run time (found via the loader's search path, e.g. `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`), but several programs can share one copy.

questions.prompt: A static library for the name `util` is a file called `libutil{{0}}`.
questions.explain: Created with `ar rcs libutil.a a.o b.o` and used with `gcc main.c -L. -lutil`.

questions.prompt: The environment variable `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` lists extra directories where the loader searches for {{0}} libraries at run time.
questions.explain: Static libraries are only needed at link time, so the loader never looks for them.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a Makefile are true?
options: A recipe line must start with a TAB character
make re-runs a recipe when one of its dependencies is newer than the target
The recipe runs once for every dependency listed
`%.o: %.c` is a pattern rule that tells make how to build any .o from the matching .c
questions.explain: A rule is `target: dependencies` followed by TAB-indented recipe lines. make compares timestamps to decide what is out of date. The recipe runs once per target, not once per dependency.
option_notes: True: that is what makes incremental builds fast.
